payload.author: Juan Lentino
payload.content:
Streaming services have started attaching consequences to AI disclosure, and so far every one of them lands on the party who answers truthfully. A declaration that used to cost nothing now has a price in one direction only.

Every penalty lands on the confession

On October 14, YouTube Music began labeling songs created primarily using generative AI. Its example is a track whose composition and vocals both came from a model. The labels draw on two inputs: what music partners declare at delivery, and YouTube's own detection tools. Partners declare through DDEX, the industry's standard format for sending release information to services, or through a spreadsheet template. They choose one of three designations, running from Fully Gen AI to No Gen AI with Partly Gen AI between them.

YouTube's announcement says nothing about what the label does to a track's recommendations or payouts. Other services have been specific. In July, TIDAL stopped paying royalties on music it identifies as wholly AI-generated, and it expects distributors to flag that content before it arrives. In September, Spotify started badging artist profiles that represent AI-generated identities, and it keeps those profiles out of editorial and algorithmic recommendations unless a listener already follows them.

Each of those consequences is triggered by exactly what a truthful declaration supplies. Take one generated track headed to TIDAL and the two answers a distributor can give.

A · Declares Fully Gen AI

Asks for zero royalties

The penalty applies on delivery, and nothing the distributor does later reverses it.

B · Declares No Gen AI

Gets paid until caught

Royalties flow until a detector disagrees, if one ever does.

The field now leans one way

Before any of this, I argued that a declaration that costs nothing to enter records very little, whether it is made or withheld. That described a field with no consequences attached. Attaching consequences leaves the field no more informative and makes it lopsided.

Honesty now has a known price. The cost of misdeclaring depends on whether a classifier notices and when, and the party misdeclaring shapes those odds by choosing what to upload. A rational supplier of generated tracks at volume answers No Gen AI, or Partly Gen AI where a flat denial looks risky, and books the expected penalty as a cost of doing business. Deezer has said that up to 85 percent of streams on fully AI-generated tracks in 2025 were fraudulent. That is the population these penalties are aimed at, and it was never going to volunteer.

The category boundaries become price boundaries at the same moment. TIDAL's penalty attaches at "wholly," YouTube's label at "primarily," and nothing published says how much human work moves a track out of either one. A vague line was tolerable when the label only informed a listener. Once the line also decides who gets paid, the vagueness is an invitation. The place that line belongs is a reading taken from a record of what happened, and for most releases that record doesn't exist.

The detector ends up deciding

Every one of these schemes keeps detection as the backstop, so every dispute over a false declaration comes down to a score. TIDAL says it will extend its tag from wholly to substantially AI-generated music once detection is reliable enough to apply it consistently. The reach of the penalty is set by a vendor's tool, not by anything the uploader can show. Each new penalty also enlarges the market detection is sold into. The more a false No is worth, the more misdeclaration there is to catch, and the vendor's business grows with the problem it is paid to contain. Deezer, the source of the 85 percent figure, announced it in January in the same release where it said it would begin selling the detection technology behind it, and the French collecting society Sacem became the first licensee.

Deezer says Billboard uses the same tool to decide which charting tracks count as AI-generated. The 99.8 percent accuracy attached to it is Deezer's own figure.

Spotify's design is the one place the honest answer gets treated differently. Its badge tells a listener whether the artist disclosed or Spotify applied the label after its own review. That distinction is real, and it is reputational only. The recommendation penalty is identical either way.

Spotify's support page names the two variants. AI Persona means the artist self-identified. Likely AI Persona means Spotify applied it after review.

The case for creation-time records in Provenance Over Detection was built for this situation. A record written while the work happens would make the false answer the expensive one, because faking it would mean fabricating evidence during the session instead of ticking a box at delivery. None of these services has said whether it would pay royalties against such a record, or weigh it above a detector's verdict.

References

Music Business Worldwide. "TIDAL to automatically tag AI-generated music and block it from earning royalties." June 2026. musicbusinessworldwide.com

Music Week. "Spotify to flag AI-generated artists with new 'AI Persona' badge." August 2026. musicweek.com

Deezer. "Deezer confirms demonetization of up to 85% of AI-music streams due to fraud and moves to sell AI-detection Technology." January 29, 2026. newsroom-deezer.com

payload.title: The honest answer now costs money
